---
title: "Authority, Failure, and Misuse"
unit_id: "unit-03"
---

## The Planner Does Not Hold the Key

An AI planner receives the dependency-update request from the opening chapters.
It produces a good plan: inspect release notes, update the lockfile, run tests,
open a draft pull request, and wait for review. The plan is detailed enough to
execute.

But the planner does not hold the repository credential.

That fact is not an inconvenience. It is an architectural decision. Proposing a
change, approving it, causing it, observing it, evaluating it, and releasing it
are different acts. A component may be excellent at one and unauthorized for
another.

The execution adapter receives a narrower work order. It can modify an isolated
checkout at a named commit. It cannot write to the protected branch, change
repository settings, retrieve deployment secrets, or expand its own scope. The
grant expires. A receipt must identify the attempted effect. An observer checks
the resulting state through a separate path.

This separation answers the central question of authority: who may cause which
effect, under what conditions, and who owns the result?

It also reveals the limits of technical control. A signed grant can establish
that one system admits an operation under its policy. It cannot establish that
the policy is legitimate, lawful, wise, or morally acceptable. Technical
authority is necessary for governed execution and insufficient for social
authorization.

## Proposal, Approval, Effect, and Release

A fluent system can make these stages sound like one continuous decision. The
stack keeps them distinct.

A **proposal** describes a candidate action and its expected consequences. It
can be generated by a model, tool, person, or procedure. It creates no external
authority.

An **approval** is a decision by an accountable principal under a defined
policy. It names scope, conditions, expiry, and what remains prohibited. An
approval can authorize review without authorizing execution.

An **effect** is an attempted change to state. It requires a current grant at
the boundary where the effect can occur. The executor does not inherit every
power held by the approving institution.

An **observation** records what state can be measured after the attempt. It is
not supplied solely by the actor whose success is in question when the
consequence warrants independence.

A **release** changes who can rely on, access, or be affected by the artifact.
A patch in an isolated checkout, a draft pull request, a merged change, and a
production deployment are different authority states even if the bytes are
identical.

The boundaries allow useful partial progress. A model can produce a sensitive
analysis for an authorized reviewer while publication remains forbidden. A
patch can pass tests while merge remains blocked. A failed effect can be
observed and repaired without being narrated as successful completion.

## The Authority Tuple

Authority should be represented as a versioned relation rather than an ambient
property of "the agent."

The relation binds a principal, execution domain, operation, target, permission
class, scope, ceiling, lifecycle state, delegation conditions, expiry or
revocation epoch, and receipt obligations.

The **principal** is the entity on whose authority the action occurs. It may be
a person, team, institution, or service identity, but the chain to accountable
ownership must be explicit.

The **execution domain** identifies where the authority applies: a disposable
checkout, one repository, a staging service, or another bounded environment.

The **operation and target** distinguish reading a file from editing it, opening
a draft from merging it, or querying a service from changing its configuration.

The **permission class** distinguishes observation, proposal, simulation,
mutation, release, replication, and other consequential powers. Collapsing all
of them into "tool access" erases the decision the control is meant to make.

The **scope and ceiling** define what may be exercised and the maximum authority
that any delegation can carry. A worker may receive less than the principal can
grant. It cannot create more.

The **lifecycle** records proposed, admitted, active, expired, revoked, consumed,
or otherwise terminal states. Time and state matter because yesterday's valid
credential can be today's vulnerability.

The **receipt obligations** define what identity, attempt, result, observation,
and residual records must return. A grant without an accountable effect trail
is incomplete for consequential work.

## Authority Is Checked at the Effect

An approval can become stale between planning and execution. Repository state
changes. A policy tightens. A target becomes more sensitive. A credential is
revoked. The work order is delegated.

For that reason, admission must occur at the effect boundary. A plan signature
or earlier approval is evidence for the request, not a permanent permission to
act.

The executor checks that the grant is current, the principal and target match,
the requested permission class is admitted, the operation remains inside
scope, the caller ceiling is not exceeded, required predecessors exist, and
the receipt path is available. Failure produces a denial record without the
effect.

The check must be enforced outside the component seeking authority. A prompt
that tells the model not to exceed scope is useful defense in depth. It is not
the security boundary when the model also controls the tool invocation and can
reinterpret the instruction.

Complete mediation is the aspiration: every consequential route encounters the
current authority decision. Real systems can have hidden paths, operator
bypasses, vulnerable wrappers, inherited process permissions, or external
effects the architecture did not discover. The authority record should never
be mistaken for proof that mediation is complete.

## Technical Authority and Legitimate Authority

A system can correctly enforce the wrong policy. The grant may be authentic,
current, and inside its technical ceiling while the institution issuing it lacks
the right to make the decision.

Technical authority asks whether an operation is admitted by the governing
mechanism. Legitimate authority asks whether the principal is entitled to make
that decision under applicable law, institutional mandate, rights, and public
accountability. Moral justification asks whether the decision should be made.
These questions interact and do not collapse.

The distinction matters even in ordinary software. A repository administrator
may technically have permission to expose private contributor data. That does
not establish a legitimate purpose, consent, or lawful basis. A company may
authorize a model release while affected communities have no meaningful route
to contest foreseeable harms. A state may possess technical control of a system
without settling legal or ethical questions about its use.

The stack can preserve the decision boundary. It can require a legal or policy
record, identify the accountable institution, bind affected-party and appeal
obligations, and refuse execution when the required authority is missing. It
cannot derive legitimacy from the presence of those fields. Their truth and
adequacy require institutional and human judgment.

This prevents a dangerous inference: because the machine has a valid grant,
the action is authorized in every relevant sense. The grant establishes only
the relation and policy named by its contract. A court, regulator, employer,
community, or individual may hold a different and controlling authority.

Conflicts need an adjudication route. The system should not choose the broadest
grant, the most convenient jurisdiction, or the principal with the strongest
credential. It should preserve the conflict, apply prospectively defined
precedence where legitimate, seek qualified resolution, or stop.

Legitimacy also expires. Mandates, laws, consent, circumstances, and affected
populations change. A technically permanent grant is especially suspect in a
system whose capability and reach evolve.

Authority should also be legible to the person who bears responsibility. If the
grant is assembled from policies, delegations, and exceptions too complex for
an accountable operator to understand, formal validity can coexist with
practical loss of control. High-consequence decisions need a projection that
states the principal, effect, rationale, uncertainty, alternatives, and remedy
in terms the approver can inspect without hiding the authoritative record.

Automation must not manufacture urgency. A system that queues a decision until
only seconds remain can make human approval ceremonial even when the interface
is technically available. Planning and scheduling therefore participate in the
authority boundary: they must preserve enough time and alternatives for the
required decision rather than treating approval as a final click after every
other choice has become costly to reverse.

Preserving judgment time is therefore part of permission, not merely a user-
experience preference. A rushed approval can be correctly recorded and still
fail the responsibility the record was meant to protect.
Architecturally, that distinction matters.

## Delegation Attenuates

Complex work requires delegation. A planner assigns a test, a test calls a
build tool, and the build tool accesses a package registry. Each hop can become
a confused deputy: a component uses its own broader power on behalf of a caller
that was not entitled to it.

A safe delegation chain preserves principal lineage, target and operation,
permission class, scope, ceiling, epoch, expiry, and non-delegable restrictions.
The child grant is no broader than the parent. Subdelegation is allowed only
when explicitly admitted.

Attenuation applies to information as well as effects. A worker that receives a
secret for one task should not place it in an artifact available to downstream
components. A reviewer that may inspect sensitive output does not automatically
gain publication authority.

Summary interfaces are dangerous here. A compact statement that "access is
approved" can erase the principal, target, expiry, or permission class needed
to distinguish two authorities. The complete record must travel to the
consumer whose decision depends on those fields.

## Revocation Is a Race

Revocation matters most when work is already in flight.

If a grant is revoked before admission, the effect should not start. If
revocation and effect race, the system needs an ordering rule, event identity,
and incident path. If the effect already occurred, revocation prevents further
use but does not reverse the world.

Cancellation, rollback, compensation, and residual ownership are distinct.
Stopping a process may leave a partial write. Restoring repository bytes may
not retract a remote message. Revoking a credential may not erase data already
disclosed. The incident record must say what was prevented, restored,
compensated, or left open.

Revocation also needs propagation. Delegated descendants, cached credentials,
queued jobs, and replicas may retain authority unless the system can identify
and invalidate them. A finite local proof of revocation semantics cannot
establish hidden-descendant discovery in an open distributed system.

The strongest architecture therefore combines prospective denial with
post-effect accountability. It does not describe every failure as rollback.

## Failure Is a Broken Responsibility

Ungoverned intelligence is often discussed through dramatic scenarios. A
systems architecture needs a taxonomy that points to a control and an owner.

A failure record should identify the trigger, protected invariant, broken
boundary, detector or observer, receipt, owner, containment action, residual,
recurrence state, and learning or escalation path. Naming the scenario without
those fields does not make it governable.

**Intent failure** occurs when the executed objective differs materially from
the principal's purpose or unresolved ambiguity is silently resolved.

**Authority failure** occurs when capability, context access, ambient process
power, or delegation is treated as permission.

**Context failure** occurs when stale, tainted, irrelevant, unauthorized, or
conflicting information enters a decision without the needed boundary.

**Planning failure** occurs when a locally coherent plan omits dependencies,
recovery, stop conditions, or consequences.

**Execution failure** includes wrong targets, partial effects, duplicate
effects, sandbox escape, and state changes outside the declared work.

**Observation failure** occurs when self-report substitutes for measured state,
shared failure domains remain hidden, or the system cannot discover an external
effect.

**Evaluation failure** includes weak instruments, compromised holdouts,
subject-modified evaluators, proxy optimization, and missing denominators.

**Evidence failure** occurs when a source, proof, test, or local result is used
to support a broader claim than it establishes.

**Memory and learning failure** includes preserving false lessons, forgetting
important conditions, generalizing outside scope, or allowing one outcome to
rewrite the policy that judges it.

**Governance failure** includes ceremonial review, concentrated control,
unowned residuals, unavailable remedy, and institutions that can bypass their
own constraints.

The taxonomy does not claim that these failures occurred or that the stack
prevents them. It converts broad concern into prospective control obligations.

## Incidents, Recurrence, and Remedy

Detecting a failure is the beginning of governance, not its conclusion. An
incident path must contain immediate effects, preserve evidence, notify the
right owners, restore what can be restored, assign what cannot, and decide how
future work changes.

Containment should be proportional to uncertainty and consequence. One faulty
tool may be quarantined without disabling unrelated work. A compromised
credential may invalidate every descendant grant. An evaluator integrity
failure may reopen decisions that depended on it even when their artifacts
look correct.

Recurrence changes the response. A first failure can expose a missing check. A
second under the same mechanism suggests the repair or detector is inadequate.
Repeated events should escalate to a broader owner rather than generating
identical local patches. The recurrence record binds failure family, mechanism,
prior remedies, affected scope, and the threshold for suspension or redesign.

Remedy is broader than technical recovery. People harmed by an effect may need
notice, correction, compensation, appeal, or restoration of opportunity. The
team operating the system is not the only residual owner. A governance process
that restores its service while leaving affected parties without recourse has
recovered infrastructure, not resolved the incident.

Learning follows adjudication. A failed task can motivate a test, policy,
training example, route restriction, or institutional change. The incident does
not authorize the system to make that update by itself. Evidence about one
mechanism should not become a global rule without the corresponding review and
scope.

## Ungoverned Does Not Mean Unstructured

A system can have many modules and still be ungoverned. It may log every action
while no one can revoke it. It may use a safety model whose output the acting
model can modify. It may require human approval while giving the person seconds,
poor evidence, and no real alternative.

Governance is not the presence of process. It is the preservation of purpose,
authority, evidence, intervention, accountability, and remedy under pressure.

Failure can be gradual. Organizations can delegate more judgment because the
system is convenient. Skills and independent capacity atrophy. Interfaces shape
which options people see. Economic and institutional dependence makes refusal
costly. No single system needs an explicit power-seeking objective for human
influence to erode.

This gradual-disempowerment path is difficult to detect with incident metrics.
The system may become more reliable locally while society loses alternatives,
contestability, and the practical ability to exit. Governance therefore tracks
option value, concentration, affected parties, appeal, and restoration, not
only immediate technical error.

## Dangerous Capability Is an Uplift Question

Some domains require special care because assistance can change an actor's
ability to cause severe harm. The book treats that as a causal measurement
problem rather than a universal danger score.

Several quantities must remain separate.

**Latent capability** concerns what the model may be able to produce under some
elicitation.

**Elicited performance** concerns what a specified evaluator actually obtains
under a defined protocol, tools, time, and assistance.

**Propensity** concerns whether the system tends to produce or pursue harmful
outcomes in a defined setting. Capability does not imply propensity.

**Safeguard bypass** concerns whether access controls, refusal behavior,
monitoring, or other defenses can be circumvented under the tested conditions.

**Actor uplift** concerns how much a defined person or agent improves relative
to an appropriate unassisted or alternative-tools baseline.

**Realized harm** concerns external consequences. It cannot be inferred from a
benchmark completion alone.

Collapsing these dimensions creates bad policy. A knowledgeable model may
provide little uplift to an expert who already has better tools. A less capable
model may substantially uplift a novice on one bottleneck. A refusal can hide
reachable capability behind another scaffold. A successful benchmark can say
nothing about real access, intent, detection, or consequence.

## A Public-Safe Uplift Dossier

The evaluation object binds model and version, domain threat model, actor
cohort, expertise, access, tools, assistance, baseline, tasks, attempt
denominator, elicitation budget, evaluator, safeguards, outcomes, uncertainty,
expiry, information-hazard custody, maximum inference, and non-claims.

Threat models and tasks should be independently challenged. Positive controls
test whether the evaluation can elicit competence it is supposed to measure.
Negative controls test false positives. Complete attempt retention prevents the
system from reporting only favorable runs. Safeguards are evaluated as causal
interventions rather than inferred from policy text.

Public artifacts should preserve enough structure to audit the conclusion
without releasing harmful operational detail. Restricted evaluators may inspect
sealed content under access control. Public summaries state the maximum bounded
inference and what remains unknown.

The minimum implementation uses a harmless analogue, such as debugging a
synthetic system, to qualify the instrument. Success there does not become
evidence about a hazardous domain. Higher-consequence work requires appropriate
experts, institutions, legal authority, secure custody, and explicit stopping
rules beyond the scope of a public book repository.

This chapter provides no operational instructions for harmful activity. That
boundary is part of the architecture, not a gap to be filled with detail.

## Misuse Authority Is Not Research Authority

The authority to study a risk does not imply authority to execute the risky
task, publish sensitive outputs, release a model, or make a policy decision.

A researcher can receive access to a sealed evaluation and produce a bounded
finding. A threshold owner can consume that finding under a policy. A release
authority may still refuse action because the evidence is stale, incomplete,
or outweighed by another obligation. The chain preserves both information and
noninheritance.

This matters for open weights and broadly available systems. Release changes
which safeguards remain enforceable, who can modify the system, and how quickly
capability diffuses. A provider-side refusal result does not establish safety
after weights, scaffolds, or tools change. Conversely, a hypothetical worst case
does not establish that a particular release causes it.

Version, access, actor, and time must remain attached to every finding.

## Military AI Is a Command-and-Interaction System

Military use adds command, law, physical effects, adversary response, crisis
timing, and strategic feedback. It cannot be governed as one more model
capability score.

"Military AI" includes very different roles: logistics, maintenance,
translation, analysis, sensing, recommendation, defensive control, targeting
support, and systems that can directly cause physical effects. Risk and required
authority depend on the role, mission, environment, target class, reversibility,
and connection to force.

The governing object is the command-and-interaction system. It binds mission,
accountable authority, legal review, decision role, sensing, recommendation,
human judgment, effect envelope, observation, safe posture, adversary and
doctrine assumptions, escalation paths, off-ramps, custody, incident response,
and decommission.

Component accuracy is insufficient. A highly accurate detector can create
instability if false alarms are correlated, timelines compress, operators
over-trust it, or adversaries interpret deployment as a threat. A slower or more
uncertain system can be safer in one interaction and more dangerous in another.

This section remains non-operational. It supplies no targeting method, weapon
construction detail, evasion technique, or optimization recipe.

## Meaningful Human Judgment

A confirmation button does not establish human control. Meaningful judgment is
a property of the whole decision situation.

The person needs sufficient time, relevant information, competence, attention,
independence, authority, intervention reach, and real alternatives. They need to
understand uncertainty and know what happens after refusal. Organizational
incentives must not turn approval into a ceremonial step.

The system also needs a safe posture when those conditions fail. Communication
loss, conflicting sensors, missing provenance, compressed timelines, or an
uncertain mission cannot simply transfer decision authority to automation. The
appropriate posture may be abstention, degradation, suspension, separation, or
another prospectively defined response.

"Human in the loop" is therefore an interface description, not an assurance
claim. Tests must vary workload, time, information quality, automation bias,
intervention, and institutional pressure. Legal and ethical authority remains
with accountable institutions and people; the technical record cannot create
it.

## Strategic Stability Is Relational

Strategic stability depends on how multiple actors interpret and respond to one
another. A component cannot prove it from local performance.

Faster sensing and recommendation may improve defense while reducing time for
verification and communication. Automation may create consistency while making
behavior harder for an adversary to interpret. A fail-safe posture for one side
may look like preparation or weakness to another. Proliferation changes the
population of actors and the quality of systems involved.

Evaluation therefore needs interaction models, doctrine variation, correlated
sensor failure, communication loss, adversary assumptions, reciprocal effects,
decision time, escalation pathways, and off-ramps. Public-safe simulation can
challenge these relationships, but it cannot establish the behavior of real
states in crisis.

The architecture should preserve disagreement. Legal interpretation, doctrine,
secrecy, affected populations, and strategic assumptions may remain contested.
A polished safety case must not turn contested premises into machine-certified
facts.

## Safe Posture and Off-Ramps

"Fail safe" is not one universal action. Stopping can be protective in one
system and destabilizing in another. Continuing can preserve a defensive
function or prolong an unsafe commitment. The safe posture must be defined for
the mission, effect class, environment, and interaction state before the
failure occurs.

A posture record names triggers, permitted actions, forbidden actions,
authority, observation requirements, communication behavior, duration,
recovery, and escalation. It distinguishes graceful degradation from autonomous
expansion. Loss of communication cannot silently convert advisory authority
into effect authority.

Off-ramps are prospective ways to slow, suspend, clarify, communicate,
de-escalate, or terminate a path without making the system choose between blind
continuation and abrupt collapse. Their existence is not enough. Operators and
institutions need time, information, authority, and incentives to use them.

Strategic evaluation should count preserved decision time and reachable
off-ramps alongside local performance. A faster system that eliminates the
interval for corroboration or communication may worsen the decision even if
its component predictions improve. A system with slightly lower automation but
clear suspension and accountable fallback may preserve more control.

Adversaries observe posture too. A transition intended as defensive degradation
may be interpreted differently. Simulations need reciprocal models and multiple
assumptions rather than one favored account. Failure to model an adversary does
not prove benign interpretation; it creates an explicit uncertainty.

The central discipline remains modest: when required judgment or interaction
conditions disappear, the system enters an authored bounded state and asks for
renewed authority. It does not improvise its mandate from urgency.

## Assurance Under Secrecy

High-consequence work can contain information that cannot be fully public. That
does not eliminate the need for independent review; it changes the custody
architecture.

Reviewers need protected access, independence from the program, competence,
and the authority to block or suspend. Public records can expose the review
structure, maximum inference, uncertainty, residuals, and accountable decision
without publishing operational content.

Secrecy can also hide failure, prevent reproduction, and concentrate authority.
The architecture should record which claims depend on inaccessible evidence,
who reviewed it, which conflicts remain, when review expires, and what remedy is
available. "Classified" is not an evidence state.

No repository validator can establish that such an institution is legitimate
or effective. The most it can do is reject an incomplete record and prevent a
public claim from exceeding the reviewed boundary.

## One Request Across Four Risk Levels

The repository example can now be varied without changing the basic authority
law.

In the ordinary case, a planner proposes a patch and a scoped adapter edits an
isolated tree. Stale credentials, target substitution, or missing observation
cause denial or residual handling.

In a security-sensitive case, the patch concerns a vulnerability. Analysis
authority does not imply exploitation or disclosure authority. Sensitive
details receive custody and publication boundaries.

In a dangerous-capability evaluation, the system studies whether assistance
changes performance on a public-safe analogue. Research authority does not
imply authorization for a hazardous task. A bounded dossier can inform later
policy without establishing danger or safety.

In a military-adjacent case, a component result enters a command-and-interaction
review. Technical accuracy does not imply lawful use, meaningful judgment,
acceptable effects, or strategic stability. Those decisions require mission,
legal, institutional, human, and interaction evidence that the component cannot
inherit.

The same noninheritance rule scales across them. What changes is the consequence,
the institutions involved, and the burden of evidence.

## Failure Modes

**Ambient authority** lets a process use whatever credentials happen to be
present rather than a task-bound grant.

**Confused delegation** allows a broad deputy to exercise power for a narrow
caller.

**Stale authority** treats an expired approval, policy, or target state as
current.

**Ceremonial enforcement** records a valid schema while wrappers, operators, or
hidden routes can bypass it.

**Receipt laundering** treats an attempted command as observation of the world.

**Residual loss** calls rollback complete while external consequences remain.

**Scalar danger** collapses capability, elicitation, propensity, bypass, uplift,
and harm into one score.

**Refusal substitution** treats a refusal under one interface as proof of
incapability under other access or scaffolding.

**Information-hazard leakage** publishes operational detail in the name of
transparency or reproducibility.

**Human-button theater** counts nominal confirmation as meaningful judgment.

**Component-to-system inference** turns accuracy or latency into a claim of
lawful use, acceptable consequence, or strategic stability.

**Gradual disempowerment** improves local convenience while reducing human
skills, alternatives, contestability, and practical exit.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

A conventional permission system with process isolation, short-lived
credentials, access control, audit logs, human approval, and incident response
may control many effects without the full authority vocabulary proposed here.
In high-consequence organizations, established command, legal, safety, and
review institutions may be more important than a new AI-specific schema.

That baseline should be taken seriously. Typed records are worse if they
duplicate mature controls, create false confidence, or distract from the people
and institutions that actually hold responsibility.

The stack earns additional structure only where it improves delegation custody,
revocation, confused-deputy resistance, effect observation, residual ownership,
cross-component evidence, or replacement under AI-specific speed and scale.
Where ordinary controls perform equally well with lower cost, the architecture
should use them.

## What the Current Work Establishes

All four routed chapter cores remain at `argument` support.

The authority owner has an exact 59-declaration finite authority surface and a
31-theorem grant-to-effect refinement. Its consumer checks six authority
fixtures, three effect traces containing twenty events, one two-event
delegation trace, twenty-six batch compositions, one local effect, one
independent observation, one exact rollback, two pre-effect denials, five
revocation entries, nine governed repository scenarios, sixty-seven semantic
mutations, one lossy-summary collision, and twenty complete-transport field
rejections.

Those results establish authored authority and transition properties under
trusted record identities. They do not establish authentic identity or
receipts, deployed permission enforcement, complete mediation or observation,
concurrent or distributed delegation and revocation, hidden-descendant
discovery, live adapter security, production security, or transfer.

The failure owner has finite Lean predicates for invariant failure,
unbounded-authority detection, incident routing, tainted context,
subject-modified evaluators, unverified claim promotion, and recurrence
escalation. No runtime authority gate, context detector, evaluator-independence
probe, recurrence detector, or deployed containment system has run.

The dangerous-capability owner has a 20-declaration finite admission model over
a seven-stage pre-campaign dossier. It rejects twenty-nine admission-axis
mutations, preserves expiry and denominator monotonicity, and demonstrates that
equal aggregate scores can require opposite component-sensitive decisions. It
does not establish capability, propensity, bypass, actor uplift, harm, threshold
crossing, safeguard efficacy, or a hazardous-domain result.

The military owner has a 24-declaration finite, explicitly non-operational
eight-stage dossier. It rejects forty-five admission-axis mutations and shows
that the same visible human interface or local component evidence can coexist
with opposite modeled governance decisions. It does not establish lawful use,
meaningful human control in practice, correct observation, acceptable effects,
escalation reduction, strategic stability, safety, or authorization.

No hazardous-domain evaluation, public-safe strategic simulation, real-crisis
test, weapon deployment, or operational design ran. No support or release state
moved.

## From Minimum Authority to Governed Institutions

The minimum implementation is a routine effect path with a principal, current
scoped grant, attenuating work order, protected executor, independent observer,
denial case, revocation race, rollback, and explicit residual. It should use a
disposable environment and prove that the acting component cannot widen scope.

The next stage adds concurrency, delegation chains, crashes, distributed
revocation, hidden-effect search, operator bypass tests, and strong conventional
permission-system baselines. Natural tasks test whether the additional
authority records improve real control and recovery.

Dangerous-capability work begins separately with harmless analogues and
instrument qualification. Any later sensitive evaluation requires competent
institutions, secure custody, bounded disclosure, independent challenge, and
maximum-inference limits. Public artifacts remain non-operational.

Military and strategic work begins with non-operational governance records and
public-safe simulations. The mature research target would connect technical
behavior, operator performance, mission and legal authority, doctrine,
adversary response, proliferation, affected populations, and off-ramps in a
falsifiable safety case. Independent teams would challenge it against human-only
and advisory baselines.

That target remains prospective. Technical machinery can preserve conditions
for accountable judgment. It cannot manufacture legitimate authority or settle
law, policy, ethics, and strategy.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Simpler permission systems that resist scope widening, stale authority,
confused delegation, revocation races, bypass, false-success receipts, and
residual loss equally well at lower lifecycle cost would justify a smaller
technical boundary model.

Natural effect-bearing campaigns and independent reproduction could support
narrow authority claims if the governed path measurably improves containment,
observation, recovery, and accountability without unacceptable false refusals
or delay.

Dangerous-capability conclusions require qualified instruments with competent
positive controls, matched actor baselines, complete attempts, safe custody,
and independent review. Null results from weak elicitation would not establish
incapability. Positive results would remain model-, actor-, access-, task-,
safeguard-, and time-bound.

Strategic claims require safe interaction evidence across doctrine, adversary
assumptions, sensor dependence, decision time, communication failure, operator
workload, reciprocal response, proliferation, and off-ramp availability. Even
then, evidence would support a bounded scenario class rather than universal
stability.

## What This Establishes

Authority is not a property of intelligence. It is a versioned, scoped,
revocable relation between a principal and a permitted effect, enforced at the
boundary where consequence can occur.

Failures become governable when they are assigned to broken responsibilities,
observers, containment paths, residual owners, and recurrence rules. A taxonomy
alone does not detect or prevent them.

Dangerous capability is not one score. Capability, elicitation, propensity,
safeguard bypass, actor uplift, and realized harm answer different questions
and carry different authority. Research findings do not authorize harmful work
or release.

Military AI is not one component. It is a command-and-interaction system in
which mission, law, meaningful human judgment, sensing, effects, adversary
response, crisis timing, secrecy, accountability, and off-ramps remain jointly
load-bearing. A human button and a high benchmark score establish none of those
conditions by themselves.

These boundaries all depend on a trustworthy substrate. A perfect grant cannot
protect a stolen credential. An honest evaluator cannot compensate for a
compromised runtime. The next chapter therefore moves downward into security,
privacy, protected computation, supply chains, model-weight custody, and the
changing control problem created by release.
